catalog_quote: 6. Stress. Stress is also non-contrastive. It may vary freely without causing ambiguity, but it is generally conditioned by one or more of several factors. If stress is defined in terms of acoustical pressure as measurable by a continuous level recorder or on a cathode-ray oscillograph, the following relations have been observed: a. An open vowel is generally more stressed than a close one. ... b. A /high/ syllable is in general more stressed than a /low/ one. ... In the following words it is the /high/ syllable which carries the heaviest stress, irrespective of its place within the word ... c. A /high + low/ syllable has usually more stress than either /high/ or /low/ syllables. ... d. A long syllable is generally more stressed than a short one ... g. sweep_summary: Kiowa (kiow1266) is in the catalog as tonal (deciding source Sivertsen 1956 sec. 6 'Stress': stress non-contrastive, freely varying). this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Miller 2015 'A Prosodic Analysis of the Word in Kiowa' (Penn WPL 21.1 art. 20; Glottolog's 'pages 20' is the article number, the paper is 10 pp). downloaded open from the Penn DSpace repository (hdl 20.500. its Tone section (p. 2) restates the H/L/HL contrast from Watkins 1984, and its only stress mention is a second-hand quotation of Crowell 1949's stress-based word definition (p. 4) with the note that Crowell's stress observations were impressionistic. Bears on catalog: confirms (tonal, no stress rule). Following that citation chain I also downloaded Crowell 1949 (IJAL 15:163-167) from the archive.org IJAL scan (scanned text, saved with a pp. 163-167 excerpt): a tentative 1947-48 auditory analysis positing four pitch phonemes plus three phonemic stress degrees, with one 'loudest' stress per word and no placement rule. On its face this contradicts the catalog's 'stress non-contrastive' coding, but it is exactly the analysis Sivertsen 1956 cites (fn. 4) and overturns instrumentally, and no later description (Watkins 1984, Jurgensen 2011, Miller 2015, Miller 2018) posits stress phonemes; so the classification stands and Crowell 1949 should be added to the bibliography as the refuted pre-instrumental analysis. Best new first-hand statement: Crowell 1949 p. 165 (does not supersede Sivertsen 1956). Nothing remains to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title (priority none for both items). access went through the Penn DSpace REST API and the archive.org metadata/download endpoints directly.

new_statements.quote: A syllable may constitute an utterance in Kiowa. When it does, it is preceded and followed by pauses, which can be called open juncture, and its linear constituents are accompanied by one member of each the following accent phonemes: Pitch: mid level (unmarked), high level (/), rising-falling (^), low (\). Stress: loudest ('), louder (''), loud (unmarked). Any syllable pattern may follow any other except that no more than two consisting of V alone succeed one another in close juncture. Phonologically, a word is a syllable or a sequence of syllables, one of which is accompanied by the loudest stress, between open junctures.

new_statements.reading: The only first-hand stress statement newly read in this search of works with stress in the title. Crowell (1949), on impressionistic auditory data, treats Kiowa as having both four pitch phonemes and three degrees of phonemic stress, with exactly one 'loudest' stress per phonological word and no rule for its position (p. 166 adds that 'stress-and-juncture patterns are morphemes' and that her intonation statements 'are impressionistic and cannot be documented at this time'). Taken alone it would code Kiowa as tonal plus lexically distributed stress. It does NOT change the catalog: the deciding source, Sivertsen 1956, cites this very paper (fn. 4) and, from oscillograph measurements of the same language, concludes 'Stress is also non-contrastive. It may vary freely without causing ambiguity' (sec. 6, p. 125), with stress statistically attracted to open, high-toned, long syllables regardless of position; Watkins 1984, Jurgensen 2011, Miller 2015 and Miller 2018 all describe Kiowa as a three-tone language with no stress phonemes. Crowell 1949 is worth adding to the per-language bibliography as the refuted pre-instrumental analysis.

sources.quote: p.43: 'Pitch is contrastive in Kiowa (high, low, and falling)... Only H and L are permitted on short vowels, while all three tones are permitted on long vowels or VC sequences when C is from the set /m, n, l, j/ (Watkins, 1984).' Minimal triplet k'O: given. Kiowa grammatical sketch has a Tone section and no Stress section (the Stress section 3.2.4.2 is for Saulteaux Ojibwe, which p.108 contrasts as 'analyzed as a stress language (not tonal)'). Ch.4 describes word-domain Tone Lowering after HL (Watkins 1984:30) but no stress process for Kiowa.

sources.quote: p. 2: 'Pitch is contrastive in Kiowa (high, low, and falling). High tone (H) is marked with an acute accent (e.g. á), low tone (L) is marked with a grave accent (e.g. à), and falling tone (HL) is marked with a circumflex (e.g. â). Only H and L are permitted on short vowels, while all three tones are permitted on long vowels or VC sequences when C is from the set /m, n, l, j/ (Watkins 1984).' p. 4: 'Crowell (1949), however, attempts to define the word in phonological terms separate from the syntax. Specifically, she argues "phonologically, a word is a syllable or a sequence of syllables, one of which is accompanied by the loudest stress, between open [pauses]" (Crowell 1949:165) ... though she concedes that all observations regarding stress and pausing are impressionistic and therefore not conclusive.'
sources.locator: sec. 2.1.3 'Tone' (p. 2); sec. 2.3 'The Kiowa Verb as a Single Word' (p. 4); secs. 3-5 (pp. 5-10)
sources.note: 'Prosodic' here means prosodic-phonology domains: the paper argues from syllable-sensitive rules (Final Devoicing, Closed-Syllable Shortening, Vowel Truncation, Glide Formation, Dental-Velar Switch) that the Kiowa verb complex consists of up to four phonological words (stem + suffixes) plus an excluded pronominal prefix. It contains no statement about stress placement and no stress rule; its only mentions of stress are the second-hand quotation of Crowell 1949's stress-based word definition (with the note that Crowell's stress observations were impressionistic) and a Turkish reference title.…
